item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q001_histone_related_proteins","answer":"In SCOPe, canonical eukaryotic core histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4—and variants such as CENP-A—belong to the Core histones family (a.22.1.1). Their broader relatives include archaeal histones in the Archaeal histones family (a.22.1.2) and histone-fold transcription-factor subunits, including histone-fold TAF pairs, NF-YB/NF-YC, and NC2 subunits, in the Histone-like transcription factors family (a.22.1.3). These families are united in the Histone-fold superfamily (a.22.1), within the Histone fold (a.22) and the all-alpha-proteins class (a). Family membership provides the strongest evolutionary relationship; shared superfamily indicates probable remote homology despite potentially weak sequence similarity, whereas fold or class membership alone would not establish common ancestry. Consequently, chromatin packaging, DNA-binding specificity, interaction partners, and transcriptional roles must not be transferred merely from the shared fold. Same-family structures are preferable templates; superfamily-level templates may support fold or domain modeling but require cautious alignment and independent functional evidence. Bacterial proteins commonly called histone-like—such as HU/IHF, H-NS, and Dps—perform partly analogous chromosome-organizing roles but have different SCOPe folds and are not histone-fold homologs. Representative comparisons should use correctly bounded domains from each relevant family rather than treating multidomain proteins or redundant structures as independent evidence.","evidence_used":["pretrained model knowledge"]}]}
